recall_prompt: Say how you would find x² + 4x — how you rewrite each term as 3·5·7… over a factorial, what you add to both sides, what you compare with, how you find p, q and y, and how 2 + x gives the answer.
insider_note: Each term is short of one factor 3 on top: rewrite 5/(2!·3) as (3·5)/(2!·3²) and p = 3 appears, not the printed 5. The missing start is 1 + 1 = 2, and the final line squares 2 + x = √27.

steps.label: Rewrite with factorials
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Each denominator is a product like 5·10·15 = 5³·(1·2·3), so every term becomes (a product)/(k!) times (1/3)ᵏ. Each term is short of one factor 3 on top: 5/(2!·3) = (3·5)/(2!·3²). Written that way the numerators are 3·5, 3·5·7, … — p = 3 — and the 1 and the (3/1!)(1/3) terms are missing, so add 1 + (3/1!)(1/3) = 2 on both sides.
lines: The 1 and the (3/1!)(1/3) terms are missing,

recall.must_convey: That the series is rewritten so the k-th term is a product over k! times (1/3) to the power k, after adding 1 + (3/1!)(1/3), which is 2, on both sides so the missing early terms are present.
accept: write each term as a product over k factorial times one by three to the power k and add 1 + (3/1!)(1/3), which is 2, on both sides
split each denominator into three to the power k times k factorial
add 1 + (3/1!)(1/3), which is 2, to both sides and bring the series to the shape one plus p by one factorial into x by q and so on
prathi term ni k factorial tho, one by three power k tho rayali, rendu sides ki 1 + (3/1!)(1/3), which is 2, add cheyali
rewrite the denominators as powers of three times factorials

steps.why: The standard expansion of (1 − y)^(−p/q) has a k! in every denominator and a fixed ratio y/q raised to k. Until the given series is written in that exact shape, p, q and y cannot be read off.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add 1 + (3/1!)(1/3), which is 2, on both sides when the series starts late, so the comparison has no 1 to match.
Writing 5·10·15 as 5·3! instead of 5³·3! — every factor carries a 3.
Losing the alternating sign when the terms alternate.

steps.label: Compare with the standard expansion
steps.margin_note: Third mark, for WRITING the standard expansion beside the series. The examiner looks for the pattern p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!. All plus signs mean the (1 − y) form.

recall.must_convey: That the series is compared with the expansion of (1 − y) to the power minus p by q, whose coefficients are p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!.
accept: compare with the expansion of (1 − y) to the power minus p by q
match it with one plus p by one factorial into y by q plus p into p plus q by two factorial into y by q squared and so on
use the standard binomial series with negative fractional index (1 − y) to the power minus p by q
(1 − y)^(−p/q) formula tho compare cheyali
the pattern p then p into p plus q over the factorials is the standard series

steps.why: This is the only binomial expansion whose coefficients grow as p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q). Naming it turns the rest of the question into reading off three numbers.
common_mistakes: Using the (1 − x) form for an alternating series or the (1 + x) form for an all-plus series.
Writing p(p + 1) instead of p(p + q) — the step between factors is q, not 1.

steps.label: Find p, q and y
steps.margin_note: Fourth and fifth marks. p is the first factor (3), p + q is the second (5) so q = 2, and y/q equals the common ratio 1/3 so y = q/3 = 2/3.

recall.must_convey: That p = 3 and p + q = 5 give q = 2, and y/q = 1/3 gives y = two by three.
accept: p is three, p plus q is five so q is two, and y by q is one by three so y is two by three
the first factor gives p equal to three and the second gives q equal to two
y by q equals one by three so y equals two by three
p three, q two vasthai, y by q one by three kabatti y two by three
read off p from the first numerator and q from the gap between the factors

steps.why: Three unknowns need three matches: the first numerator fixes p, the second fixes p + q, and the ratio inside the bracket fixes y/q. Nothing else in the series is free.
common_mistakes: Taking y = 1/3 directly — the bracket holds y/q, so y = q × 1/3.
Reading q from the second factor as a whole instead of as p + q.

steps.label: Evaluate the power
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Substitute p, q, y into (1 − y)^(−p/q) and simplify the fraction inside the bracket before touching the exponent.

recall.must_convey: That substituting gives two plus x equals three to the power three by two, which is root twenty seven.
accept: substituting gives two plus x equals three to the power three by two, which is root twenty seven
put the values into (1 − y)^(−p/q) and simplify to get two plus x equals three to the power three by two, which is root twenty seven
the bracket becomes one by three and the power gives two plus x equals three to the power three by two, which is root twenty seven
values substitute cheste two plus x equals three to the power three by two, which is root twenty seven vasthundi
simplify the bracket first then apply the negative index
heard_as: two plus x equals three to the power three by two, which is root twenty seven

steps.why: A negative index inverts the fraction and a fractional index takes a root. Doing the inversion first keeps the root over a simple fraction.
common_mistakes: Inverting the exponent instead of the fraction when the index is negative.
Leaving a root in the denominator without a clear final value.

steps.label: Square and rearrange
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. 1 + 1 + x = 2 + x. Square it: x² + 4x + 4 = 27, and the 4 moves across.

recall.must_convey: That 2 + x = √27, so (2 + x)² = 27 gives x² + 4x + 4 = 27 and x² + 4x = 23.
accept: two plus x is root twenty seven so squaring gives x squared plus four x plus four is twenty seven and the answer is twenty three
square two plus x to get twenty seven then subtract four to get twenty three
x squared plus four x equals twenty three

the answer is twenty three

steps.why: x² + 4x is (2 + x)² − 4. The series gives 2 + x directly, so the answer needs one squaring and one subtraction.
common_mistakes: Adding only 1 on both sides and missing the (3/1!)(1/3) = 1 term, which changes the left side to 1 + x.
Reading p as 5 from the printed first numerator instead of 3 after the rewrite.
